idiom_name: execute-around helper or try/finally around the acquisition; TS 5.2 using / await using with Disposable and AsyncDisposable on supporting runtimes
implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript's runtime, so there is no destructor: the classic owner structure is replaced by a callback bracket (one function acquires, runs the body and releases in a finally) or an explicit try/finally, and TypeScript's contribution is at the type level - TS 5.2 added the using/await using declarations and the Disposable/AsyncDisposable interfaces built on Symbol.dispose/Symbol.asyncDispose, which give the C#-style deterministic close where the target runtime provides those symbols (or the compiler's downlevel helpers plus a Symbol.dispose polyfill). Because the declaration needs runtime support and older engines lack it, a library keeps the callback form as its public API and uses the declaration only where the project's target guarantees it; a value merely annotated as Disposable is not checked at run time.
pitfalls: await using is required for asynchronous teardown: with a synchronous using (or a try/finally missing await) the close is not awaited and the next statement races the release.
using needs Symbol.dispose at run time and the esnext.disposable lib; compiling to an older target does not create the symbol, so a project without a polyfill throws at the declaration.

Types do not enforce the protocol: a cast or an interface from a dependency can claim Disposable while the value has no [Symbol.dispose], and the failure only appears when the declaration runs - validate foreign values at the boundary where they are wrapped.
